column1: “Tinubu has borrowed ₦120 trillion, more than everyone before him!”
column2: I understand why that number worries people. But a big part of it isn't new loans. When the naira fell, the dollar debts we already owed got bigger in naira. In dollars, our debt went from about $113 billion to $121 billion. The real question is what the loans are building, and we should all demand to see that.
column3: Presidency, 8 Nov 2026. Debt rose from ₦87.38tn to ₦166.79tn in naira terms; ₦22.7tn was old Central Bank overdrafts now counted as debt.

column1: “Why is he still borrowing after removing the subsidy?”
column2: Fair question. Removing the subsidy reduced how much the country would otherwise have had to borrow, but it didn't end borrowing, because other costs rose too: wages, debt payments and infrastructure. The campaign supports publishing exactly what each loan is paying for.
column3: Finance Ministry: ₦30.64tn extra spending pressures vs ₦20.4tn extra FG resources (June 2023–Dec 2025).

column1: “Most of our money goes to paying debt.”
column2: That's a real pressure; debt service took about two-thirds of federal revenue in 2025. Much of that comes from old debts and a weaker naira. It's exactly why reforms to raise revenue and stabilise the naira matter.

column1: What is the difference between "new borrowing" and "debt growth"?
column2: Debt growth also includes inherited debt being recorded, refinancing, and exchange-rate revaluation of old foreign loans. New borrowing is only fresh loans. Critics often present all debt growth as new borrowing.
column3: ₦22.7tn of inherited Ways and Means (CBN overdrafts) was converted to recorded debt.
